title: How to Tell If There Is Mold in Your Air Ducts
h1: How to Check Your Air Ducts for Mold
description: Musty smells, dark spots around vents and worse allergies can point to mold in air ducts. Learn how to check safely and what to do if you find growth.
quick_answer: Signs of mold in air ducts include a musty smell when the system runs, dark spotting on or around vent covers, visible growth inside return grilles or near the AC coil, and allergy-like symptoms that ease when you leave the house. You can check vents with a flashlight, but confirming and removing mold deeper in the system takes a professional inspection.
body:
What causes mold in air ducts?

Mold needs moisture, and ducts usually stay dry. When mold shows up, something is adding water. Common causes include:

  • A clogged condensate drain or overflowing drain pan at the air handler
  • Condensation on uninsulated or poorly insulated ducts running through a hot attic
  • Leaky supply ducts that sweat where cold air meets warm attic air
  • An oversized AC that cools quickly but doesn't remove enough humidity
  • Roof leaks or plumbing leaks that drip onto ductwork
  • High indoor humidity, especially in homes near the coast

This matters because cleaning mold without fixing the moisture source only buys time. It will grow back.

What are the signs of mold in ducts?

  • A musty smell that gets stronger when the heat or AC turns on
  • Dark spots or speckling on supply vent covers or the ceiling around them
  • Visible growth on the inside of a return grille, the filter frame or the duct lining
  • Allergy symptoms like stuffy noses, headaches or itchy eyes that improve when you're away from home
  • Water stains on ceilings near the air handler or along duct runs

Keep in mind that dark spots on vent covers can also be dust or soot, especially after wildfire smoke or candle use. Not every dark mark is mold.

How can you check your ducts yourself?

You can do a basic visual check without special tools:

  1. Turn off the system at the thermostat.
  2. Remove a supply vent cover and the return grille.
  3. Shine a bright flashlight into the duct as far as you can see.
  4. Look at the filter and its frame for fuzzy growth or discoloration.
  5. Check the area around the air handler in the attic, garage or closet for standing water, rust or stains.
  6. Smell the air near the vents right after the system starts.

Wear a dust mask and gloves, and don't scrape or disturb anything that looks like mold. Disturbing it releases spores into the air.

What should you avoid doing?

  • Spraying household bleach or cleaners into the ducts. They can damage duct materials and won't reach most of the growth.
  • Running the system on high to air it out, which just spreads spores through the house.
  • Using foggers or scented products that cover the smell without fixing the cause.
  • Pulling apart flexible ducts in the attic, which can tear the liner and insulation.

What does a professional mold inspection and cleaning involve?

A technician starts by finding where the moisture comes from. That usually means checking the drain line and pan, duct insulation, coil condition and system sizing. A camera inspection can show what's happening deeper in the ducts where a flashlight won't reach.

If growth is found, the affected area is cleaned under negative pressure so spores are captured, not spread. Badly contaminated flexible duct is often replaced rather than cleaned, since its inner liner is hard to clean thoroughly. The moisture problem is fixed, and the system may be treated with an EPA-registered product suited for HVAC use.

Our air duct cleaning service includes this kind of inspection. If mold keeps coming back, our indoor air quality team can look at humidity control and UV lights near the coil.

How do you keep mold from coming back?

  • Have the condensate drain flushed during each tune-up
  • Repair or replace ducts with damaged insulation in the attic
  • Seal leaky duct joints so warm, moist attic air can't get in
  • Keep indoor humidity moderate, and use bathroom and laundry fans
  • Change filters on schedule, since a damp, dirty filter can grow mold
  • Fix roof and plumbing leaks quickly

Coastal homes in particular benefit from paying attention to humidity. A little prevention keeps a small spot from turning into a whole-system problem.

If you've just moved into a home, or the system sat unused for a long stretch, an inspection is a smart first step. Musty smells the first time the AC runs in spring are common in coastal homes, and they're often the earliest clue that moisture has been collecting somewhere in the system.
faqs: Can mold in air ducts make you sick?

Mold can trigger allergy and asthma symptoms in sensitive people, such as congestion, coughing and itchy eyes. If anyone in the home has ongoing symptoms, talk with a doctor and have the system inspected.
Is black dust around vents always mold?
No. Dark buildup around vents is often dust, soot from candles or wildfire smoke, or dirt pulled through leaky ducts. A closer inspection can tell the difference.
Can I clean mold out of my ducts myself?

Small surface spots on vent covers can be cleaned, but mold inside the ducts should be handled by professionals with negative-pressure equipment. DIY cleaning often spreads spores and misses the moisture source.
Will a UV light prevent mold in ducts?
A UV light near the AC coil helps keep mold from growing on the coil and drain pan, which are common trouble spots. It won't fix a moisture problem in the ducts themselves.
